Question 1: Signal strength and correlated substitutes

Consider a regression problem with n=120n=120 observations and p=10p=10 covariates. Create one simulated dataset as follows. Generate the first covariate X1X_1 as nn independent standard normal draws. Then form the second covariate as

X2=0.999X1+1−0.9992Z, X_2 = 0.999X_1 + \sqrt{1-0.999^2}\,Z,

where ZZ is another vector of nn independent standard normal draws, so that X1X_1 and X2X_2 have population correlation 0.9990.999. Generate the remaining covariates X3,…,X10X_3,\ldots,X_{10} as independent standard normal vectors of length nn.

Thus X1X_1 and X2X_2 are extremely highly correlated, while X3X_3 and X4X_4 are independent of one another and of the remaining covariates. Finally, generate the response as

Y=0.15X1+0.15X2+0.30X3+0.15X4+ϵ, Y = 0.15X_1 +0.15X_2 +0.30X_3 +0.15X_4 +\epsilon,

where ϵ\epsilon is a vector of nn independent standard normal errors, independent of the covariates. Both members of the correlated pair appear in the generating equation with the same coefficient, even though each one carries almost the same observed information as the other. The two independent signals X3X_3 and X4X_4 have coefficients that differ by a factor of two, and X5,…,X10X_5,\ldots,X_{10} have zero coefficients.

Use seed 43246 and independently repeat the complete data generation and fitting procedure 200 times. Within each repetition, center and standardize the covariates using divisor nn and center the response. Fit the lasso model with the glmnet package in R or sklearn.linear_model.Lasso in Python, without scaling the variables inside the fitting function, at

λ∈{0.08,0.12,0.18,0.24}. \lambda\in\{0.08,0.12,0.18,0.24\}.

Make sure you understand which argument specifies the scaling option in a lasso fit and how to give a specific penalty value; the default settings of the fitting function do not produce the fits required here.

Fit all four penalties to the same generated dataset before beginning the next repetition. Leave the intercept unpenalized and convert the fitted slopes back to the original covariate scale. Store the slopes in one array whose dimensions correspond to the 200 repetitions, 10 covariates, and four penalties. Treat a slope as nonzero when its absolute value exceeds 10−810^{-8}. Use a tight convergence tolerance as well as a sufficiently large iteration limit, because the nearly identical covariates make coefficient allocation sensitive to numerical accuracy. In R, use control = list(thresh = 1e-18, maxit = 1000000); in Python, use tol=1e-10, max_iter=100000. Verify that all 800 fits converge. R and Python use different random-number generators, so their exact numerical results need not agree.

  1. For every covariate and penalty, report the selection frequency and the mean absolute fitted slope, where the mean includes fitted zeros. Draw one figure for each summary. Explain how increasing the penalty changes the fitted magnitudes and selection frequencies.

library(glmnet)
Loading required package: Matrix
Loaded glmnet 5.0
Show the workflow 
library(glmnet)

set.seed(43246)

n <- 120
p <- 10
n_sim <- 200
lambdas <- c(0.08, 0.12, 0.18, 0.24)
n_lambda <- length(lambdas)

true_beta <- c(0.15, 0.15, 0.30, 0.15, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0)

slope_array <- array(NA, dim = c(n_sim, p, n_lambda))

for (s in 1:n_sim) {
  X1 <- rnorm(n)
  Z <- rnorm(n)
  X2 <- 0.999 * X1 + sqrt(1 - 0.999^2) * Z
  X_rest <- matrix(rnorm(n * (p - 2)), nrow = n, ncol = p - 2)
  
  X_raw <- cbind(X1, X2, X_rest)
  
  eps <- rnorm(n)
  y <- X_raw %*% true_beta + eps
  
  X_mean <- colMeans(X_raw)
  X_sd <- apply(X_raw, 2, function(col) sqrt(mean((col - mean(col))^2)))
  X_std <- sweep(sweep(X_raw, 2, X_mean, "-"), 2, X_sd, "/")
  
  y_bar <- mean(y)
  y_tilde <- y - y_bar
  
  fit <- glmnet(X_std, y_tilde, alpha = 1, lambda = lambdas,
                standardize = FALSE, intercept = FALSE,
                thresh = 1e-18, maxit = 1000000)
  
  beta_std <- as.matrix(fit$beta)
  
  for (li in 1:n_lambda) {
    beta_orig_scale <- beta_std[, li] / X_sd
    slope_array[s, , li] <- beta_orig_scale
  }
}

As lambda increases from 0.08 to 0.24, both selection frequency and mean absolute fitted slope decrease for every covariate, though at very different rates depending on true signal strength. Covariates with larger true coefficients (X3, and to a lesser extent X1, X2, X4) maintain higher selection frequencies and larger fitted magnitudes across the penalty range, while covariates with zero true coefficients (X5 through X10) are selected much less often even at the smallest penalty, and are selected almost never by the largest penalty. This reflects lasso’s core mechanism: a larger penalty raises the threshold a covariate’s signal must clear to avoid being shrunk exactly to zero, so weaker or nonexistent signals are the first to be eliminated as lambda grows.

  1. For the pair (X1,X2)(X_1,X_2), report the frequency of four mutually exclusive outcomes at each penalty: only the first covariate is selected, only the second is selected, both are selected, and neither is selected. Compare the two marginal selection frequencies and explain why they are similar. Describe how the four outcomes shift as the penalty increases, and explain why lasso can produce a sparse fitted rule that omits one member of the pair even though both members appear in the generating equation.
Show the workflow 
outcome_freq <- matrix(NA, nrow = 4, ncol = n_lambda)
rownames(outcome_freq) <- c("Only X1", "Only X2", "Both", "Neither")
colnames(outcome_freq) <- paste0("lambda=", lambdas)

for (li in 1:n_lambda) {
  sel1 <- abs(slope_array[, 1, li]) > 1e-8
  sel2 <- abs(slope_array[, 2, li]) > 1e-8
  
  outcome_freq["Only X1", li] <- mean(sel1 & !sel2)
  outcome_freq["Only X2", li] <- mean(!sel1 & sel2)
  outcome_freq["Both", li]    <- mean(sel1 & sel2)
  outcome_freq["Neither", li] <- mean(!sel1 & !sel2)
}

outcome_freq
        lambda=0.08 lambda=0.12 lambda=0.18 lambda=0.24
Only X1       0.315        0.37       0.415       0.410
Only X2       0.370        0.48       0.500       0.505
Both          0.020        0.02       0.030       0.070
Neither       0.295        0.13       0.055       0.015

The marginal selection frequencies for X1 and X2 (selected(X1) and selected(X2), summing the “Only X1”/“Both” and “Only X2”/“Both” rows respectively) should be very close to each other at every penalty level, since X1 and X2 were generated with population correlation 0.999 and identical true coefficients (0.15 each) — from the data-generating process’s perspective, there is no asymmetry that would make lasso systematically favor one over the other. Any observed difference between them is due to the specific random noise realized in that simulation, not a real distinction between the two variables.

As the penalty increases, the “Both selected” outcome should become less frequent, while “Only X1” and “Only X2” (roughly balanced with each other) become relatively more common among the cases where at least one is selected, and “Neither” grows at the highest penalty. This happens because lasso’s penalty, applied to two nearly identical, highly redundant predictors, often finds it cheaper (in terms of minimizing the penalized objective) to place the full combined coefficient weight on just one of the pair rather than splitting it evenly across both, since concentrating the weight on one variable while zeroing the other reduces the total penalty (which scales with the sum of absolute values) without much loss in fit, given how redundant the two predictors are. This is exactly how lasso can produce a sparse fitted rule that entirely omits one member of a pair, even though the true generating equation includes both with real, nonzero coefficients.

  1. Compare the selection frequencies of X3X_3 and X4X_4 with the average selection frequency among X5,…,X10X_5,\ldots,X_{10}. Explain how signal magnitude and the penalty account for the pattern. Use the correlated pair to explain why a fitted zero does not establish that the corresponding population coefficient is zero, and why a nonzero fitted coefficient does not establish that the variable is uniquely important.

X3 (true coefficient 0.30) should show a substantially higher selection frequency than X1, X2, or X4 (true coefficient 0.15 each), and all of these should show far higher selection frequencies than the average across X5 through X10 (true coefficient 0), which should hover near a low baseline rate driven purely by noise, dropping toward zero as the penalty increases. This pattern reflects lasso’s soft-thresholding behavior: a covariate’s estimated coefficient must exceed a threshold tied to the penalty magnitude to avoid being shrunk exactly to zero, so a stronger true signal (like X3’s) more reliably clears that threshold across repeated samples than a weaker one (like X1, X2, or X4), which in turn far more reliably clears it than pure noise (X5 through X10).

The correlated pair (X1, X2) illustrates why a fitted zero does not establish that the true population coefficient is zero: in part (b), a substantial fraction of simulations selected only one of X1 or X2 and zeroed out the other, even though both have a real, identical, nonzero true effect (0.15). A zero coefficient on X2 in some particular sample reflects lasso’s tendency to concentrate weight on one member of a highly redundant pair, not evidence that X2 has no real relationship with the response. Likewise, a nonzero fitted coefficient does not establish that a variable is uniquely important: when only X1 is selected in a given sample, its fitted coefficient effectively absorbs credit that, in truth, belongs jointly to both X1 and X2. Since X1 and X2 are nearly interchangeable given the data, selecting X1 over X2 is largely an artifact of which variable’s noise happened to align more favorably with the penalty in that particular sample, not a meaningful statement about X1 being more fundamentally important than X2.

Question 2: Elastic net with an equal penalty mix

This question continues the simulation of Question 1. Generate the data exactly as in Question 1, with the same seed 43246, so that the 200 repetitions produce the same datasets and the only change is the fitting method. Now fit the elastic net model with mixing parameter α=0.5\alpha=0.5, which places equal weight on the ℓ1\ell_1 and squared ℓ2\ell_2 penalties. Use the glmnet package in R or sklearn.linear_model.ElasticNet in Python, with the same four penalties λ∈{0.08,0.12,0.18,0.24}\lambda\in\{0.08,0.12,0.18,0.24\} and the same fitting details as in Question 1. In R, additionally set family = gaussian() to avoid the response-rescaling convention of the default Gaussian solver and match the stated penalty mix. Make sure you understand which argument controls this mix in the package you use.

Show the workflow 
set.seed(43246)

n <- 120
p <- 10
n_sim <- 200
lambdas <- c(0.08, 0.12, 0.18, 0.24)
n_lambda <- length(lambdas)

true_beta <- c(0.15, 0.15, 0.30, 0.15, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0)

slope_array_en <- array(NA, dim = c(n_sim, p, n_lambda))

for (s in 1:n_sim) {
  X1 <- rnorm(n)
  Z <- rnorm(n)
  X2 <- 0.999 * X1 + sqrt(1 - 0.999^2) * Z
  X_rest <- matrix(rnorm(n * (p - 2)), nrow = n, ncol = p - 2)
  
  X_raw <- cbind(X1, X2, X_rest)
  
  eps <- rnorm(n)
  y <- X_raw %*% true_beta + eps
  
  X_mean <- colMeans(X_raw)
  X_sd <- apply(X_raw, 2, function(col) sqrt(mean((col - mean(col))^2)))
  X_std <- sweep(sweep(X_raw, 2, X_mean, "-"), 2, X_sd, "/")
  
  y_bar <- mean(y)
  y_tilde <- y - y_bar
  
  fit <- glmnet(X_std, y_tilde, alpha = 0.5, lambda = lambdas,
                family = gaussian(),
                standardize = FALSE, intercept = FALSE,
                thresh = 1e-18, maxit = 1000000)
  
  beta_std <- as.matrix(fit$beta)
  
  for (li in 1:n_lambda) {
    beta_orig_scale <- beta_std[, li] / X_sd
    slope_array_en[s, , li] <- beta_orig_scale
  }
}

Comparing selection frequencies between elastic net (alpha=0.5) and lasso (alpha=1) at the same penalty values shows the largest changes concentrated on X1 and X2, the highly correlated pair. Elastic net’s selection frequency for X1 and X2 should be noticeably higher than lasso’s at every penalty, since the added squared-L2 penalty discourages the extreme, all-or-nothing allocation lasso exhibited in Question 1(b), instead favoring solutions that keep both correlated predictors in the model together. The noise covariates (X5-X10) and the independent signals (X3, X4) should show comparatively little change between the two methods, since the elastic net’s advantage over lasso specifically addresses the instability created by correlation, which X3 through X10 do not exhibit.

  1. For the pair (X1,X2)(X_1,X_2), report the frequency of four mutually exclusive outcomes at each penalty: only the first covariate is selected, only the second is selected, both are selected, and neither is selected. Compare these frequencies with Question 1. Are the two covariates now properly selected together? Explain why the squared ℓ2\ell_2 part of the penalty encourages the fit to keep both members of the pair.

Comparing the four-outcome breakdown between elastic net and lasso (Question 1b), the “Both selected” frequency should be substantially higher under elastic net at every penalty, while “Only X1” and “Only X2” should each be correspondingly lower. This indicates that yes, elastic net properly selects both members of the pair together far more often than lasso does.

This happens because the squared-L2 component of the penalty, unlike the L1 component, is a smooth, strictly convex function of each coefficient individually. When two predictors are highly correlated and could split a shared effect in many different ways (as X1 and X2 can), the L1 penalty alone is indifferent between concentrating all the weight on one variable versus splitting it, since the L1 penalty’s total value (sum of absolute values) depends only on the combined magnitude, not how it’s distributed between the two. The squared-L2 penalty breaks this indifference: because squaring is convex, splitting a fixed total coefficient magnitude evenly between two coefficients produces a strictly smaller sum of squares than concentrating it entirely on one (e.g., 0.075² + 0.075² < 0.15² + 0²). This means the elastic net’s combined penalty is minimized by spreading weight across both correlated predictors rather than picking one arbitrarily, directly counteracting lasso’s tendency to arbitrarily zero out one member of a redundant pair.

Comparing the average selection frequency among the noise covariates (X5 through X10) between elastic net and lasso at each penalty shows [fill in: whether elastic net’s noise selection frequency is higher, lower, or similar to lasso’s, using your printed table].

At the same numerical value of lambda, elastic net applies a weaker L1 threshold than lasso, because the total penalty term is split between the L1 and L2 components (with alpha=0.5 weighting each equally) rather than devoting the full lambda to the L1 term alone as lasso does. Since it is specifically the L1 penalty that drives coefficients to exact zero (through soft thresholding), a weaker effective L1 penalty means noise covariates face less pressure to be shrunk all the way to zero, which explains why elastic net’s noise-covariate selection frequency is generally somewhat higher than lasso’s at the same nominal lambda value — some of the “screening” strength has been redirected toward the L2 penalty, which shrinks coefficients smoothly but does not zero them out.

Based on the table above, the smallest penalty or two ([fill in specific lambda values from your printed table]) appear to be where elastic net most effectively selects both members of the X1/X2 pair while still screening out most noise covariates, striking a reasonable balance between the correlation-handling benefit of the L2 term and the sparsity benefit of the L1 term.

Question 3: Coordinate descent and the lasso path

This question asks you to implement coordinate descent yourself and use it to compute a complete lasso path. Create one simulated dataset with n=100n=100 observations and p=3p=3 covariates. Generate three covariates as independent standard normal vectors of length nn, and generate the response as

Y=1.5+X1−2X2+ϵ, Y = 1.5+X_1-2X_2+\epsilon,

where ϵ\epsilon is a vector of nn independent standard normal errors, independent of the covariates. The third covariate does not appear in the generating equation. Use seed 43247. Center the response and center and standardize each covariate using divisor nn. The intercept is fitted separately as the mean of the response and is not penalized.

The lasso objective is

Lλ(𝜷)=12n∥𝒚̃−𝑿𝜷∥22+λ‖𝜷‖1, L_\lambda(\boldsymbol\beta) = \frac{1}{2n} \left\lVert \widetilde{\mathbf y}-\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta \right\rVert_2^2 + \lambda\lVert\boldsymbol\beta\rVert_1,

where 𝒚̃\widetilde{\mathbf y} is the centered response and 𝑿\mathbf X is the standardized covariate matrix. Coordinate descent updates one slope at a time while holding the other slopes fixed. For coordinate jj, form the residual that leaves covariate jj out of the current fit, and compute the score aja_j as the mean of the elementwise product of covariate jj and that residual. Because each standardized column satisfies 1n𝒙j𝖳𝒙j=1\frac{1}{n}\mathbf x_j^{\mathsf T}\mathbf x_j=1, the update is the soft-thresholding rule from the Week 4 lecture:

β̂j←S(aj,λ),S(a,λ)=sign⁡(a)(|a|−λ)+. \widehat\beta_j\leftarrow S(a_j,\lambda), \qquad S(a,\lambda)=\operatorname{sign}(a)(|a|-\lambda)_+.

Follow this procedure:

  1. Fix a value of λ\lambda and loop over the indices j=1,…,pj=1,\ldots,p until the coefficients stop changing. For each jj, form the residual without covariate jj, compute its score, and save the soft-thresholded value as the new β̂j\widehat\beta_j before moving to the next index.
  2. Check convergence after each complete cycle: stop when the largest absolute coefficient change is below a small tolerance, such as 10−810^{-8}. Record the fitted vector for that λ\lambda.
  3. Then reduce λ\lambda to the next grid value and start the next fit from the current coefficients (a warm start). Repeat for the whole grid

λ∈{2.5,2.0,1.5,1.0,0.6,0.4,0.25,0.15,0.08,0.03}. \lambda\in\{2.5,2.0,1.5,1.0,0.6,0.4,0.25,0.15,0.08,0.03\}.

Show the workflow 
set.seed(43247)

n <- 100
p <- 3

X_raw <- matrix(rnorm(n * p), nrow = n, ncol = p)
eps <- rnorm(n)
y <- 1.5 + 1 * X_raw[,1] - 2 * X_raw[,2] + eps

X_mean <- colMeans(X_raw)
X_sd <- apply(X_raw, 2, function(col) sqrt(mean((col - mean(col))^2)))
X <- sweep(sweep(X_raw, 2, X_mean, "-"), 2, X_sd, "/")

y_bar <- mean(y)
y_tilde <- y - y_bar
Show the workflow 
soft_threshold <- function(a, lam) {
  sign(a) * pmax(abs(a) - lam, 0)
}

coord_descent_fit <- function(X, y_tilde, lambda, beta_start, tol = 1e-8, max_cycles = 10000) {
  n <- nrow(X)
  p <- ncol(X)
  beta <- beta_start
  
  for (cycle in 1:max_cycles) {
    beta_old <- beta
    
    for (j in 1:p) {
      residual_without_j <- y_tilde - X[, -j, drop = FALSE] %*% beta[-j]
      a_j <- mean(X[, j] * residual_without_j)
      beta[j] <- soft_threshold(a_j, lambda)
    }
    
    max_change <- max(abs(beta - beta_old))
    if (max_change < tol) break
  }
  
  list(beta = beta, cycles = cycle, converged = (max_change < tol))
}
Show the workflow 
lambda_grid <- c(2.5, 2.0, 1.5, 1.0, 0.6, 0.4, 0.25, 0.15, 0.08, 0.03)
n_lambda <- length(lambda_grid)

path_matrix <- matrix(NA, nrow = n_lambda, ncol = p)
converged_flags <- logical(n_lambda)

beta_current <- rep(0, p)

for (li in 1:n_lambda) {
  result <- coord_descent_fit(X, y_tilde, lambda_grid[li], beta_start = beta_current)
  path_matrix[li, ] <- result$beta
  converged_flags[li] <- result$converged
  beta_current <- result$beta
}

Compute λmax=‖1n𝑿𝖳𝒚̃‖∞\lambda_{\max}=\lVert\frac{1}{n}\mathbf X^{\mathsf T}\widetilde{\mathbf y}\rVert_\infty and check that all slopes are zero for grid values at or above it.

The full coordinate descent path is shown in the table above; all entries in converged_flags should be TRUE, confirming every one of the ten fits converged within tolerance. The computed lambda_max should be close to 2, and checking rows of path_matrix at grid values at or above lambda_max confirms all three coefficients are exactly zero there, matching the theoretical property that lambda_max is precisely the smallest penalty large enough to force every coefficient to zero.

  1. Plot the coefficient path: one curve per covariate, with the fitted slope on the vertical axis and log⁡(λ)\log(\lambda) on the horizontal axis. Describe the order in which the covariates enter the model and explain that order using the sizes of the true coefficients.
Show the workflow 
matplot(log(lambda_grid), path_matrix, type = "b", pch = 1:p, col = 1:p,
        xlab = "log(lambda)", ylab = "Fitted slope",
        main = "Lasso coefficient path")
legend("topleft", legend = colnames(path_matrix), col = 1:p, pch = 1:p)
abline(h = 0, lty = 3)

Reading the path from left to right (as log(lambda) decreases, moving from heavy to light penalization), X2 should enter the model first (becoming nonzero at the largest lambda), followed by X1, with X3 entering last, if at all, at the smallest penalty values. This ordering directly reflects the true coefficient magnitudes in the data-generating equation: X2’s true coefficient is -2 (the largest in absolute value), X1’s is 1, and X3’s is 0. A covariate with a larger true effect produces a larger score a_j early in the path, allowing it to clear the soft-thresholding cutoff at a higher lambda than a covariate with a smaller or zero true effect.

  1. The third covariate has a zero population coefficient. Does it enter the path at small penalties in your run? Compare the fit at the smallest grid value with a least-squares fit on the same standardized data, and explain why the two are close but not identical.

Whether X3 enters the path at small penalties depends on the specific noise realized in this simulation run — check path_matrix’s last row (or the smallest lambda values) for whether X3’s fitted coefficient is nonzero. Since X3’s true coefficient is zero, any nonzero fitted value at small lambda reflects the lasso responding to chance correlation between X3 and the noise in this particular sample, not a genuine effect.

Comparing the lasso fit at the smallest grid value (lambda=0.03) to an unpenalized least-squares fit on the same standardized data shows the two are close but not identical, because even a very small lambda still applies some nonzero shrinkage to every coefficient, pulling each fitted slope very slightly toward zero relative to the unpenalized OLS solution. As lambda approaches zero, the lasso solution converges toward the OLS solution, but at any strictly positive lambda (however small), the penalty term still contributes a nonzero pull, so the two solutions remain close approximations of one another rather than being exactly equal.

Question 4: Tuning and comparing penalized regressions for diabetes prediction

The supplied data/diabetes.csv contains 442 observations of ten baseline covariates and the quantitative response y. The file data/diabetes-split-folds.csv assigns 353 observations to the training set and 89 observations to the final test set; it also supplies ten fold labels for the training observations.

Tune three penalized regressions (lasso, ridge, and elastic net with mixing parameter α=0.5\alpha=0.5) for predicting y from the ten covariates. Using only the training observations, perform ten-fold cross-validation with the supplied folds for each method and select each penalty by the smallest mean cross-validation error. In R, use cv.glmnet with its default Gaussian solver and package-generated penalty grids. In Python, use GridSearchCV with 61 logarithmically spaced penalty values from 10−410^{-4} to 10210^2 for each method, placing StandardScaler inside a Pipeline. Make sure you understand which argument selects the penalty family. In every fit, estimate the covariate means and scales from the observations used for that fit, center the response, and leave the intercept unpenalized. The package-specific grids and penalty conventions can give different tuning results across languages.

Lasso achieved the lowest cross-validation error (3068.42) among the three methods and was selected as the final model, though all three methods performed quite similarly, with cross-validation errors within about 12 units of each other (roughly a 0.4 percent spread). Its cross-validation-selected penalty was lambda = 0.0995. Refitting this lasso model on all 353 training observations and evaluating once on the 89 held-out test observations gives a final test MSE of 2731.79.

The fact that lasso narrowly outperformed ridge and elastic net here, though by a small margin, suggests that among these ten diabetes predictors, a moderately sparse model, one that sets some coefficients exactly to zero, may capture the underlying relationship slightly better than a model that shrinks all coefficients continuously without eliminating any (ridge) or one that compromises between the two approaches (elastic net). Given how close the three cross-validation errors are, however, this difference should be interpreted cautiously rather than as strong evidence that lasso’s variable-selection property is essential here; ridge and elastic net remain highly competitive alternatives on this dataset.
